procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 06.06.2016 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in PIL No. 32 of 2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court declined to entertain a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) seeking to reopen the Mahatma Gandhi assassination case based on new research. The PIL raised questions about the number of bullets fired and requested the opening of the Kapur Commission Report after 46 years.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Dr. Pankaj Kumudchandra Phadnis, the petitioner in person, filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court dismissed the SLP, stating that there was no merit in it. The Court held that criminal cases concluded long ago, even those resulting in convictions, executions, and life sentences, should not be reviewed. It also stated that new research does not justify re-initiating criminal investigations and that the attempt to reopen the controversy was an exercise in futility.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Court should exercise its jurisdiction to examine the correctness or fairness of the findings in a report concerning contentious issues.

facts: A petition was filed seeking to re-examine the findings of the Kapur Commission Report concerning the Mahatma Gandhi assassination.
The petitioner specifically challenged a finding about Shri Savarkar, arguing it was unfair because he had been acquitted in the criminal trial and the finding was made after his death.
law: The Court cited the precedent from the Constitution bench case of *Ram Kishan Dalmia v. Justice S.R.Tendolkar*.
This precedent establishes that a Commission of Inquiry has no judicial or adjudicatory power, and its reports are purely recommendatory and not enforceable on their own (*proprio vigore*).
Statements made before a Commission of Inquiry are inadmissible in any future civil or criminal proceedings.
application: The Court stated that entering into the correctness or fairness of the report's findings would be an "exercise in futility" and would ignite new controversies.
It reasoned that the Court must be wary of such contentious issues and should not allow its jurisdiction to be invoked for such purposes.
Applying the legal precedent, the Court noted that the Commission's finding was merely a "general observation" and could not overturn the criminal court's acquittal of Shri Savarkar.

Since the report is only recommendatory and has no binding legal effect, the Court found no point in examining its findings, as any redress or punishment must be decided by a court of law based on its own discretion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request to examine the correctness or fairness of the report's findings, concluding that such an exercise would be futile, would stir unnecessary controversy, and was legally pointless given the non-binding and purely recommendatory nature of a Commission of Inquiry's report.

issue.issue_text: Whether the 'nation's right to know the truth' can be invoked to reopen settled issues based on academic research raising a different perspective.

facts: A petitioner, based on his own academic research, sought to reopen the criminal investigation into the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi, which had been concluded 70 years prior.
The original case resulted in convictions and the execution of sentences, and all the accused persons are no longer alive.
The petitioner argued that the 'nation's right to know the truth' justified reopening the case to investigate a different perspective suggested by his research.
law: While the nation has a right to know the truth, this right is not absolute.
There is no provision in law to review or reopen criminal cases that have been long concluded, especially when convictions have been upheld and sentences served.
Reopening settled issues based on a different perspective from academic research would amount to acting on hearsay.
Courts must be wary of being used to reopen contentious historical issues, as it would be an 'exercise in futility'.
application: The Court acknowledged the principle of the 'nation's right to know the truth' but stated it cannot be invoked when the 'truth is already well known' through a concluded judicial process.
It reasoned that the petitioner's 'new research' was not a sufficient legal basis to re-initiate a criminal investigation into a matter settled 70 years ago.
The Court determined that entertaining such a petition would be a futile exercise that would only stir up new controversies without any legal justification.
It concluded that allowing the case to be reopened based on a different academic perspective would be equivalent to reopening issues based on hearsay.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the 'nation's right to know the truth' cannot be used to reopen a long-settled criminal case simply because academic research raises a different perspective, as there is no legal provision for such a review and it would be a futile exercise based on hearsay.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Court should exercise its jurisdiction to examine the correctness or fairness of the findings in a report concerning contentious issues.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner implicitly argued that the Court should exercise its jurisdiction to re-examine the findings of past reports on contentious historical issues to correct the record and establish the truth.
respondent_arguments: The Court should not allow its jurisdiction to be invoked for such purposes, as it would be an 'exercise in futility' and would stir up new controversies.
Findings from a Commission of Inquiry are inadmissible in evidence in any future civil or criminal proceedings, making a re-examination legally pointless for securing redress or punishment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the 'nation's right to know the truth' can be invoked to reopen settled issues based on academic research raising a different perspective.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner propounded a 'fourth bullet theory', suggesting the existence of a second assailant, as a new perspective that justifies reopening the settled controversy.
The petitioner's submission that Shri Savarkar was held guilty for the murder of Gandhiji was presented as a fact needing correction.
respondent_arguments: The Amicus Curiae submitted that a perusal of the original evidence (photograph at the museum) does not support the 'fourth bullet theory'.
The theory contradicts the original trial record, where neither the prosecution nor the defence suggested that four bullets were fired or that there was a second assailant.
Any new expert statement about the photograph would be inadmissible at this late stage, especially since the person who took it cannot be examined.
The petitioner's submission that Shri Savarkar was held guilty is a misplacement of facts.

cases.case_name: Ram Kishan Dalmia v. Justice S.R.Tendolkar
cases.principle: The findings of a Commission of Inquiry have no power of adjudication, cannot be enforced 'proprio vigore' (by its own force), and cannot overturn a criminal court's acquittal. Statements made before such a commission are inadmissible in future proceedings, and a court of law must exercise its own discretion without being influenced by the commission's views.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The nation's right to know the truth cannot be invoked to reopen well-known issues merely on the basis of academic research that presents a different legal perspective, as this would be equivalent to reopening issues based on hearsay.
obiter: The Court's jurisdiction should not be invoked for contentious issues that would result in an exercise in futility and stir new controversies.
A Commission of Inquiry has no power of adjudication to pass an order that can be enforced proprio vigore.
A statement made before a Commission of Inquiry is wholly inadmissible in evidence in any future civil or criminal proceedings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court will not exercise its jurisdiction to re-examine the correctness or fairness of findings in a report on contentious historical issues, especially when prompted by academic research raising a different perspective. Such an exercise is considered futile, legally pointless because the findings of a Commission of Inquiry are inadmissible in subsequent legal proceedings, and socially disruptive as it would stir new controversies.
legal_tests_applied: The findings of a Commission of Inquiry have no power of adjudication and cannot be enforced proprio vigore.
Statements made before a Commission of Inquiry are wholly inadmissible in evidence in any future civil or criminal proceedings.
why_appellant_lost: While the nation has a right to know the truth, such a right cannot be invoked where the truth is already well known merely because some academic research raises a different perspective in law, as this would amount to reopening issues based on hearsay.
A finding from a Commission of Inquiry cannot have the effect of overturning the finding of a criminal court which acquitted a person.

There can be no point in a Commission of Inquiry making recommendations for securing redress or punishment, as such actions must be imposed by a court of law without being influenced by the Commission's views.
why_respondent_won: The Court should not allow its jurisdiction to be invoked for examining the correctness of a report on contentious issues, as it would be an 'exercise in futility' and would 'pan new fires of controversy'.

The statement made by any person before the Commission of Inquiry is wholly inadmissible in evidence in any future proceedings, civil or criminal, making a re-examination legally pointless for securing redress or punishment.
policy_considerations: This Court must at all cost be vary of such contentious issues and must not allow its jurisdiction to be invoked for such purposes.
Entering into the correctness or fairness of the findings in this report... would be another exercise in futility and would none the less pan new fires of controversy.
